prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision measurement of time and frequency

statement.case_for: Reading all eight ballots, B005 is the one entry that every colleague placed in the top four, seven of eight in the top three, and the agreement rests on arguments I can check against my own criteria rather than on shared taste. The magic-wavelength lattice is a simple mechanism with a clean theoretical idea: choose the trapping wavelength so that the light shift cancels, keep the Lamb-Dicke regime so motional shifts vanish, and then average over thousands of atoms. It is understood quantitatively (blackbody, lattice and collisional shifts are controlled and cross-checked), it has been confirmed independently by JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST and others at the 1e-18 level, and it reaches into new physics through relativistic geodesy, searches for varying constants and dark-matter signals. The attribution is as bounded as these things get: Katori proposed the scheme and built the first strontium clock, and Ye's group drove it to record accuracy and many-body control. I ranked it third in my opening only because I was drawn to the universality arguments of B016 and the novelty of B014; after reading colleagues, I judge that a prize for B005 is the most defensible and the least contested choice on the table.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty and kind. The 2005 prize (Hall, Haensch, frequency combs) and the 2012 prize (Wineland and Haroche, trapped-ion control) already cover the neighbouring ground, and a skeptical reader can see the lattice clock as a superb refinement of a precision-measurement lineage, an engineering triumph rather than a discovery about nature. There is also a timing argument for waiting for the redefinition of the SI second, and the credit for the single-ion and lattice proposals by other groups (and for experimental co-workers such as Takamoto, Ludlow and Hinkley) is not fully captured by two names. I think the first point is answerable, because the clock rests on a distinct idea, but I do not consider it settled.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B005 first as atomic physics at its most elegant, with exceptional theory-experiment agreement, but flags that overlap with the Hall-Haensch comb prize and the Wineland ion-control prize may make some colleagues see it as incremental.
responses.response: I take the overlap worry seriously but I come out where you do. The comb is a ruler and the ion clocks use single trapped particles; the lattice clock's contribution is a different mechanism, namely cancelling the trapping light shift at the magic wavelength so that many neutral atoms can be interrogated without motional shifts. That is what moves the stability and accuracy by orders of magnitude, so I read it as an independent invention, not an incremental step. Where I would push you is on the phrase 'theory-experiment agreement': the systematic shifts are controlled by calculation and cross-checked between labs, and I would like the citation to emphasise the mechanism, not just the accuracy figure.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks Car-Parrinello (B043) first as an original method that underpins computational materials science, and asks whether a method counts as a physical discovery given the overlap with the 1998 chemistry prize for DFT. He also ranks B014 second and B020 third.
responses.response: I agree that B043 is conceptually clear and enormously used, but I do not think it should be our lead this year, and your own caveat is the reason: the committee would be asking whether a computational method is a discovery of nature, and the DFT overlap with chemistry weakens the case, so it is a harder sell than a measurement that tests physics. On B014 I share your admiration, and I would keep it as my first alternative. But your own maturity note, that the pairing mechanism and sample variability are unresolved, is why I would not put it first: a prize should rest on an interpretation that has stopped moving, and for moire matter it is still moving.

responses.point: Johansson ranks B015 first for cold atoms in optical lattices (Zoller, Greiner, Bloch), arguing that it is mature, robustly confirmed and distinct from the 2001 BEC prize, and that B005 is also a clean two-person prize.
responses.response: I do not dispute that B015 is scientifically strong, and I admit that I put it last of my eight, partly out of unease about the four-name allocation (you yourself note that Esslinger and Jaksch are excluded by the three-person cap). My concern is that the stated payoff, a solution of open Hubbard-model questions such as d-wave superconductivity, has not yet been delivered, so the recognition would be of a platform rather than of a result. B005 has the opposite profile: the instrument has already delivered the promised measurement, and the credit divides cleanly into two. I would take your point that the Mott-transition work is robust and more distinct from the 2001 prize than I first allowed.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron optics (B051) first as an instrument invention of decisive impact, with Rose, Haider and Urban as a natural trio, while acknowledging a possible field bias and a credit question over the STEM corrector work.
responses.response: I agree that sub-angstrom imaging changed what materials physics can see, and I value that you flagged your own affinity. My difficulty is the same as the one you raise: the STEM-corrector credit (Krivanek, Dellby) cuts directly across the Rose-Haider-Urban trio, and, as with all instrument prizes, the committee must decide whether the mandate is met by the tool or by the discoveries it enabled. B005 is also an instrument-driven prize, so I cannot claim consistency by exclusion; the difference I would draw is that the lattice clock embodies a new physical idea whose performance tests fundamental physics directly, whereas B051 is an engineering solution to a lens-aberration problem, however brilliant.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as a discovery in the Nobel sense or as precision engineering following the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Whether to wait for the SI second redefinition before recognising the invention, and whether that would add maturity or merely delay.
Whether the credit for the lattice-clock idea and its demonstration is fully captured by Katori and Ye, given other early lattice-clock groups and Ye's co-workers.

My own first choice B016 (KPZ) has no support among colleagues, and I have not independently verified the experimental record (for example Takeuchi-Sano) against the whole literature, so I may be over-weighting a topic from my own field.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B005. For B016 (KPZ) my own research is in nearby non-equilibrium statistical physics, but I have no recorded collaboration with Kardar, Zhang or Spohn. I am in the same Gothenburg physics environment as Johansson and Olsson (Chalmers), which is institutional proximity only.
